newsitem.title: UK: Scotland's coronation stone home after 700 years.
newsitem.headline: Scotland's coronation stone home after 700 years.

text.p: Scotland's ancient Stone of Scone, stolen by an English king 700 years ago, returned to its homeland on Saturday in a ceremony bursting with national pride that refuelled the debate over independence.

The 458-pound (200 kg) slab of rough sandstone was placed in Edinburgh Castle to the sound of a 21-gun salute after being driven through the Scottish capital on a Land Rover past some 10,000 cheering Scots.
"Basically people are glad to see the Stone returning. It's a symbol of Scotland's nationhood and Scottish sovereignty," Scottish National Party (SNP) leader Alex Salmond told reporters.

"However, I think if you walked along this crowd and asked people what they would like, they would like the symbol returned but also they want the substance and the substance is a free parliament for a free people," Salmond added.

It is believed the stone was first used in the coronation of a Scottish king in 839 in the village of Scone. It served as the coronation stone for all subsequent Scottish kings until Edward I arrived from England in the 13th century to subdue Scottish rebels and seize their national symbol.
Since 1296, the stone has lain under a throne in London's Westminster Abbey, where England's kings and queens have traditionally been crowned.
It was stolen from London in 1950 by four students campaigning for Scottish independence but returned four months later.
Prime Minister John Major, who is firmly against granting Scotland independence from the rest of Britain, bowed last year to long-standing demands for the stone's return.

Major's Conservative Party, facing nationwide elections before May 1997, is deeply unpopular in Scotland although the the opposition Labour Party has promised a referendum on independence if it wins power.
Salmond said the return of the stone showed that government in London was reponding to pressure for change.

"Our task now is to ensure that the ancient nation of Scotland becomes a real nation with a government of our own choice and a voice in the international community -- to get the substance of nationhood back, not just the symbols," he said.
